ISS · engine & parser reference

Working with the C++
API reference

The canvas is a structured editor over a recognized slice of ordinary C++. The code is the source of truth: nothing the canvas shows exists only in a database, and nothing you write by hand is off-limits to the parser. That makes two contracts worth knowing before you touch a .cpp:

  1. The marker contract — which text the canvas may rewrite, and which text is yours forever.
  2. The recognized slice — the exact C++ forms the parser reads back, so a hand-written block shows up on the canvas with its ports, its messages and its state instead of as an opaque box.

Everything below is the engine as it actually is (engine/include/microarch/), not an idealized version of it.

engine/include/microarch/*.hpp packages/host/src/parser/facts.ts packages/host/src/writer/ packages/host/src/project/run.ts

1Project layout

A block's id is its dot-path (CPU0.IF), which is its namespace path plus class name. That id is the engine identity: Component("CPU0.IF"). The display label in the inspector is a separate, cosmetic thing kept in the sidecar: a Component("…") string that differs from the id is read back as that label, while one that equals the id is identity and the canvas shows the leaf name (§7).

2The marker contract

The canvas only ever splices the text between the markers (packages/host/src/writer/markers.ts). What that means per file type:

FileGenerated regionHand-owned
src/<Leaf>.cppthe whole classanything above BEGIN / below END
src/<Router>.cppctor + flat() default; the class stays open across ENDlatency models + the closing };
src/<Gen>.cpp (traffic, generated mode)the whole file, prologue includednothing — the file is canvas-owned
src/<Gen>.cpp (traffic, custom mode)class head onlytick() and the closing brace
src/<Leaf>.svmodule header + port listthe behavioral body + endmodule
inc/iss_events.h, inc/iss_arch.hthe whole bodyanything outside the markers
src/iss_main_gen.cppthe entire file — it carries markers but is rewritten whole, not splicednothing

A file with no markers at all is never rewritten — it is a hand-written file, and the canvas treats it as read-only (dashed border, "hand-written" badge, edits refused).

The router trick. In src/<R>.cpp the generated region opens class R2 : public microarch::Router { and does not close it. Your latency models sit below the END marker inside that same class body, followed by the };. That is why they survive regeneration.

3Engine API

Include the umbrella header — it pulls in everything:

Generated blocks instead include the legacy shims infra/component.h, infra/event.h, infra/link.h, which hoist the same types into the global namespace (using Component = microarch::Component;). Both work; new hand-written code should prefer microarch/engine.hpp and qualify explicitly.

3.1 Component — a block

Non-copyable. Each cycle runs dispatch → settle → tick; settle() may request more delta-cycles within the same cycle (bounded by the scheduler's maxDeltaCycles, default 1024). Only components registered with Scheduler::addClocked get settle/tick.

In practice you do not hand-write this: inc/iss_events.h is generated from the ✉ Messages view, and the bits value is derived there from the declared field types. Write messages by hand only in a project you are not authoring through the canvas.

3.3 Link — a wire

send() schedules delivery at scheduler.deliveryCycle(latency) and emits a HopRecord when a hop sink is installed — that is the seam the trace animation rides. Always guard on connected(), not destination(): a fabric-routed port intentionally has no destination.

3.5 Scheduler — the clock

Two subtleties that bite:

  • Token inheritance is automatic. Any event a handler sends inherits the in-flight token, so a trace threads into per-transaction chains for free. A component that originates traffic from its own tick() has no in-flight token — call mintToken() and assign ev->token yourself.
  • releaseActiveEvent() is how you keep an event. By default the dispatch loop frees the event after handler() returns. A handler that parks a packet (as Router does) must take ownership first; it returns null outside Dispatch or if something already took it.

3.6 Router — the fabric, and what a packet costs

Bandwidth is bits per output port per cycle (default default_event_bits = 32, i.e. one ordinary word). A packet costs Event::bits, so a 512-bit packet on a 128 b/cy port occupies it for four cycles while several narrow packets share one. Unspent budget carries while the port has a backlog and is zeroed when it drains, so an idle port cannot bank bandwidth for a burst. Weighted is bit-quantum deficit round-robin: equal weights split bits, so an origin sending 4×-wide packets gets a quarter as many of them.

Ingress resolution: a packet arriving with an empty finalDest takes the first matching rule (message type + inclusive [lo, hi] address range). No match → dropped and reported through the divergence sink with kind "drop". The simulation continues; real fabrics surface decode errors, they don't halt.

Latency models are ordinary member functions on your router subclass:

Signature must be exactly Cycle name(const Event&) (optionally microarch::-qualified) for the parser to list it in the router's inspector. Assign one per routed wire in the wire panel; unassigned wires use flat().

3.7 Trace records

Metric kinds emitted today, all by Router: qdepth (settled per-port depth, change-only), flow (packets forwarded this cycle), bits (their total width), stall (full-queue retries). JsonlTraceWriter turns all three into the JSONL the IDE reads; addr is written as a hex string, never a number, because uint64 does not survive JavaScript's 2^53.

4What the canvas reads back

This is the recognized slice (packages/host/src/parser/facts.ts). Write any of these forms and the canvas sees it; write something else and the block still compiles and runs — it just shows up with less detail.

#C++ formBecomes
S1class X : public Componenta block (struct, final, and microarch::-qualified bases all match)
S2: Component("label") in a ctor init listthe block's label
S3class E : public Event { … }a message + its payload fields
S4Link* member; / Link& member;an out-port named member
S6port->configureOut(registry.find("Y"))a wired edge to Y (Tier 1)
S6port->configureOut(&y)a wired edge — but see the caveat below
S7port->latency = N / port->setLatency(N)the wire's latency
B1make_unique<E>() … port->send(std::move(v))the port emits E
B1port->send(std::make_unique<E>(…)) / port->send<E>(…)same
B2static_cast<E&>(ev) / dynamic_cast<E&>(ev)the block consumes E
B2void handler(E& ev) — a typed handlerthe block consumes E
B2ev.type() == "E"the block consumes E
V1<type> <name> [= init]; at class depth 1a state variable
H1namespace NS { … }hierarchy — ids become dot-paths (CPU0.IF)
—Cycle name(const Event&) on a Router subclassa latency model

Notes that matter:

  • Prefer registry.find("Full.Id"). The destination of a configureOut must match a block id exactly. configureOut(&y) contributes the variable name y, so it only resolves when that variable happens to be named for the block it points at; otherwise the edge is still drawn, but with no destination (visible rather than silently dropped). The registry form names the id directly and always resolves.
  • handler(Event&) is excluded from consume detection — the base dispatch signature is not a claim about a message type.
  • Facts in free functions are dropped on purpose. A wiring call in a standalone main() is not attributed to any block; blocks own their wiring.
  • Facts merge across files: a class declared in inc/X.h collects facts contributed by src/X.cpp.
  • The parser scans inc/ and src/ (recursively) for .h .hpp .hh .cpp .cc .cxx, skipping node_modules, build, out.

How an out-port becomes an edge

TierConditionRendered
1 wiredan explicit configureOut factsolid
2 inferredthe port's message has exactly one consumer elsewheredashed
2b unresolvedseveral candidate consumers, no wiringred, to: null
routedthe port is fabric-bound; a router rule resolves it per packetorchid, ⇢ via R1
3 stubmessage emitted, nobody consumes it (or no send on the port)dotted

Tier 1 always wins. If a wire you drew disappeared, check that configureOut survived your edit; if an edge you expected never appeared, check that the destination actually consumes the message in one of the three B2 forms.

Give a message an honest width. Widths come from the declared field types (uint64_t data[8] costs 512 bits). When the field list can't express the truth — a compressed payload, an unnamed header, a burst that is one logical packet — set the override in the ✉ Messages view rather than editing iss_events.h, which is regenerated.

6Build and run

▶ Run (or build/design <cycles>) compiles with:

Which files become translation units:

  • src/iss_main_gen.cpp — always.
  • Any top-level src/*.cpp that contains no marker — i.e. your hand-written files, compiled as their own TUs.
  • Generated block files are not TUs. They are single-file inline classes #included by the harness, which is why they carry #pragma once.

Two consequences worth stating plainly:

  • A hand-written .cpp inside a subdirectory (src/CPU0/Mine.cpp) is neither compiled as a TU nor included by the harness. Put hand-written blocks at the top level of src/, or include them from a file that is.
  • The harness only instantiates blocks that are in the model (the sidecar). A hand-written class is parsed and drawn on the canvas, but nothing constructs, wires or clocks it unless the design authors it.

The run writes iss_trace.jsonl next to the binary; that file is what the canvas animates.

Verified gotcha. Adding a canvas block whose id equals a hand-written class's id does not adopt that file — it appends a generated class to it, giving you two definitions of the same class and a compile error. Give the canvas block a different id, or convert the file yourself by adding the marker region and letting the canvas own it.

7Editing rules of thumb

  • Inside a marker region, edit through the canvas. Anything you type there is gone at the next edit.
  • Below the END marker, write whatever you want — router latency models, a custom tick(), helpers, the SV twin's behavior.
  • Component("<id>") is engine identity, not a label. Renaming it renames the block in the registry, the harness wiring and every trace record. Rename through the inspector instead.
  • Constructors take their out-links positionally, in writer order. If you hand-edit a generated ctor's parameter list, the harness will pass links in the old order.
  • setLink(const char* port, Link*) is the stable ABI for injecting a link after construction; prefer it over reaching into members.
  • Keep uint64_t addresses out of any JSON you emit yourself — write them as hex strings, as the trace writer does.

Source of truth for everything above: engine/include/microarch/*.hpp (the API), packages/host/src/parser/facts.ts (the recognized slice), packages/host/src/writer/ (what is generated and how it splices), and packages/host/src/project/run.ts (the build). When this document and those files disagree, they are right.
